QUESTION:
Is Prednisone safe to use during pregnancy?

RESPONSE:
Short answer: the excerpt you provided (Indications and Dosage & Administration sections only) does not contain any pregnancy information, so I can't quote the label on this point. Here is general prescribing information about prednisone in pregnancy, but your obstetrician or prescriber should make the final call for your situation.

Key points generally found in prednisone labeling and clinical practice:

• Prednisone is not absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. It is commonly used when a pregnant person has a condition (e.g., asthma flare, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disease, transplant) where untreated illness poses a greater risk to mother and baby than the drug does. Corticosteroid labels typically say it should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.

• Corticosteroids cross the placenta. Prednisone/prednisolone cross relatively poorly compared with dexamethasone or betamethasone (much is inactivated by placental 11β-HSD2), which is why prednisone is often preferred when treating the mother rather than the fetus.

• Animal studies have shown teratogenic effects (including cleft palate, growth restriction) at high doses. Human data have suggested a small possible increase in oral clefts with first-trimester exposure, though more recent studies have not consistently confirmed this; the absolute risk, if any, appears small.

• Other considerations with prolonged or higher-dose use in pregnancy: possible fetal growth restriction, maternal gestational diabetes, hypertension/preeclampsia, infection risk, premature rupture of membranes, and rarely neonatal adrenal suppression. Infants born to mothers who received substantial corticosteroid doses during pregnancy should be observed for signs of hypoadrenalism.

• Principles that apply: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time, don't stop abruptly after long-term therapy (taper), and expect that stress doses may be needed around delivery if the HPA axis is suppressed.

• Breastfeeding: prednisone/prednisolone appear in breast milk in small amounts and are generally considered compatible with nursing at usual doses.

Bottom line: prednisone is frequently used in pregnancy when clearly needed, but it is not risk-free. Do not start, stop, or change the dose without talking to your healthcare provider, and check the full FDA-approved labeling (Use in Specific Populations / Pregnancy section) for the specific product you have.
